**Autocomplete competes with the user's typing speed.** A suggestion arriving after the user has already written the next line is wasted work, even if the completion is excellent. The design must optimize the time from the current editing state to the first useful visible suggestion, not only tokens generated per second.

**Break down one interaction.** The editor detects a stable pause, selects nearby code and relevant repository context, sends a request, the model processes that context, and the editor displays a completion. Network transit and context preparation consume part of the same latency budget as inference. A large model's benchmark latency alone does not establish that the whole feature meets a 150 ms target.

**Cancel stale work.** If the user types or moves the cursor, the old request may no longer match the file. Attach a document revision/cursor identity and discard stale responses. Otherwise the system can insert syntactically valid code into the wrong location. Cancellation also preserves server capacity.

A small nearby model, bounded context, warm workers, and reusable prefixes can help. Speculative decoding can help under suitable acceptance and batching conditions, but it is not automatically a solution to network or queueing delay. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192)

**Evaluate usefulness, not just acceptance.** Users may accept a suggestion and immediately edit or delete it. Measure retained useful code, latency, interruption rate, and correctness in supported languages. Cache only under an identity that includes relevant model and document context, so speed does not come from reusing an incompatible completion.

**Technical details and references.**

Make the latency budget explicit from keystroke to visible completion: debounce/network, context selection, prefill, and first useful output. Under a sub-150ms p95 target, use a nearby small code model, short bounded context, cached repository summaries, and aggressive cancellation of stale requests. A distant large model with cold prefill may simply not meet the target; measure components before promising it.

Context includes prefix/suffix around the cursor, imports, nearby definitions, selected open files, and retrieved symbols with repository permissions. Build a fill-in-the-middle prompt using the model’s actual training format. Cache AST/symbol indexes incrementally by file version; never reuse a completion after its surrounding code changes without revalidation.

Speculative decoding can reduce expensive verification rounds when draft acceptance is high, but draft overhead can lose at short completions. Stream complete useful fragments, suppress obviously invalid insertions, and stop on edit/cursor changes. Evaluate acceptance and accepted characters, edit distance after acceptance, syntax/test outcomes, latency, and distraction rate. Randomize experiments by user/repository to limit contamination from repeated suggestions.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** End-to-end latency includes context preparation, network transit, prefill, decoding, and rendering. These components may overlap, so use traces instead of summing unrelated percentile measurements. Cache reusable prefixes and cancel stale work; otherwise a high-throughput backend can spend most of its capacity generating suggestions the user has already made irrelevant. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/github-copilot/how-github-copilot-is-getting-better-at-understanding-your-code/) and [2](https://github.blog/2023-05-17-inside-github-working-with-the-llms-behind-github-copilot/).
